102001: Foundation models are large models pretrained on broad data at scale that can be adapted to many downstream tasks, instead of training a bespoke model per task. They changed AI engineering because one model plus prompting, retrieval, or fine-tuning now covers chat, extraction, coding, and reasoning. Engineering work shifted from training models from scratch to orchestrating, evaluating, and safely deploying them.
102002: An LLM is a deep Transformer trained on massive text corpora to predict the next token, which forces it to learn grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and world knowledge. At inference it generates text autoregressively, one token at a time, conditioned on the prompt and its own output so far. Scale of parameters, data, and compute is what makes emergent capabilities appear.
102003: After you hit enter, the app sends your message plus conversation history to the model, the text is tokenized into IDs, the model runs a forward pass producing logits, sampling with temperature and top-p picks the next token, and generation repeats autoregressively until a stop condition. The service streams tokens back while the provider orchestrates batching, KV caching, and rate limits.
102004: The Transformer is an architecture built entirely on attention with no recurrence: self-attention layers mix information across tokens in parallel, feed-forward networks transform each position independently, residual connections and normalization stabilize deep stacks, and positional encodings inject token order. Encoder variants understand text, decoder variants generate it, and encoder-decoder models translate or summarize.
102005: The key components are token embeddings plus positional encodings, stacked blocks of multi-head self-attention and feed-forward networks with residuals and layer normalization, and for decoders a masked attention so positions cannot see the future. The final layer projects hidden states to a vocabulary logits distribution for next-token prediction.
102006: Tokenization splits raw text into subword units and maps them to integer IDs the model consumes. Subwords balance vocabulary size with sequence length, handling rare words by decomposition. Byte-pair encoding and variants dominate because they never fail on unseen characters.
102007: BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) starts with characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into new tokens until a target vocabulary size is reached. Common words become single tokens while rare words split into meaningful pieces, giving a fixed-size vocabulary that can encode anything, including code and emoji, when run at byte level.
102008: WordPiece, used by BERT, greedily builds subwords maximizing likelihood and marks continuations with ## prefixes; SentencePiece treats the raw text, including spaces, as a byte stream so language-agnostic tokenization never needs pre-tokenization and can invert cleanly. Both achieve robust subword segmentation; SentencePiece is more common in multilingual LLMs.
102009: Positional encoding adds order information to token embeddings because attention is permutation-invariant: without it, 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look identical. Options include fixed sinusoids, learned absolute embeddings, and relative schemes like RoPE that rotate queries and keys.
102010: Embeddings are dense vectors that represent items, words, sentences, or users, such that geometric proximity reflects semantic similarity. They are produced by trained encoders and power semantic search, clustering, recommendation, and RAG retrieval via cosine or dot-product similarity.
102011: Q, K, V are three learned projections of each token: the Query encodes what the token is looking for, the Key what it offers for matching, and the Value the content it contributes. Attention scores come from Q-K similarity, then act as weights mixing the V vectors, allowing learned asymmetric information routing between positions.
102012: Self-attention lets every position in a sequence attend to all positions in the same sequence: each token's query is compared with all keys, the softmaxed similarities weight the values, and each output is a context-aware mixture. It gives O(1) path length between any two tokens and full parallelism across positions, which is why Transformers replaced RNNs.
102013: Cross-attention attends from one sequence to another: queries come from the decoder stream while keys and values come from the encoder outputs. It is how translation models align output words to input words and how multimodal models fuse text queries with image features. Self-attention, in contrast, operates within a single sequence.
102014: Dot products grow with dimension, so without scaling, large d_k pushes the softmax into saturated regions where gradients vanish. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) normalizes the score variance to be independent of head dimension, keeping softmax sharp enough to be useful but smooth enough to learn.
102015: Causal masking sets attention scores from position i to any j > i to negative infinity before the softmax, so each token can only attend to itself and the past. This enforces the autoregressive property: training on all positions in parallel remains valid because no position sees the future, exactly matching generation-time behavior.
102016: Multi-head attention runs several attention maps in parallel on smaller projected subspaces, concatenates the heads, and applies a final projection. Different heads specialize in different relations, such as syntax, coreference, or local patterns, increasing expressiveness at nearly the same compute cost as one big head.
102017: The feed-forward network is a two-layer MLP applied to every position independently, typically expanding to 4x the model width and applying a non-linearity. It stores much of the model's factual knowledge and transforms each token after attention has mixed context, adding per-position compute capacity.
102018: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in one request: prompt plus generated output must fit inside it. It matters because everything the model can use must be present in that window; long documents get truncated or require chunking, retrieval, or summarization strategies. KV cache memory also grows linearly with context length.
102019: The context window is limited by the quadratic compute of self-attention in training, the linearly growing KV cache memory at inference, and the positional scheme's trained maximum. Attention over very long contexts also degrades in quality, with middle information getting lost, so practical limits are set by cost and effectiveness, not just architecture.
102020: Temperature divides the logits before softmax: below 1 sharpens the distribution making output more deterministic and focused, above 1 flattens it making output more diverse and creative but riskier. At 0 it is greedy decoding, picking the single most likely token. Use low temperature for extraction and code, higher for brainstorming.
102021: The first token is slow because of prefill: the model must process the entire prompt through all layers before emitting anything, with no KV cache for the prompt yet. Subsequent tokens are faster, one matrix multiply per token reusing the cached keys and values. This is why time-to-first-token grows with prompt length.
102022: Top-k sampling keeps only the k most probable next tokens and renormalizes; top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, so the candidate count adapts to distribution sharpness. Top-p is usually preferred because a fixed k is too wide for flat distributions and too narrow for peaked ones.
102023: Logits are the raw, unnormalized scores the final linear layer produces for every vocabulary token. Softmax converts them to probabilities; sampling strategies, temperature, top-k, and top-p all reshape that distribution before the next token is chosen. Training minimizes cross-entropy against these logits.
102024: Residual connections add each block's input to its output, giving gradients a direct path backward through identity branches. This prevents vanishing gradients in deep stacks, lets layers learn incremental refinements rather than full transformations, and is essential to training very deep Transformers.
102025: Open-source (open-weight) models like Llama publish weights you can host, fine-tune, and inspect, giving control over data privacy, latency, and cost at scale, but you operate the infrastructure. Closed models like GPT-4 offer top capability with zero ops burden and fast updates, but data leaves your perimeter and per-token costs apply. Choose based on privacy, volume, latency, and capability needs; many products mix both.
102026: Encoder-only models like BERT use bidirectional attention and are pretrained to understand text, excelling at classification, NER, and embeddings. Decoder-only models like GPT use causal attention and generate autoregressively, powering chat and code. Encoder-decoder models like T5 combine both, mapping input sequences to output sequences for translation and summarization.
102027: KV cache stores each layer's keys and values for previously processed tokens so autoregressive decoding reuses them instead of recomputing over the whole prefix for every new token. It turns per-token cost from growing with sequence length into constant, at the price of GPU memory that grows linearly with context and batch size.
102028: KV cache compression reduces the memory footprint through quantizing the cache to 8 or 4 bits, multi-query or grouped-query attention that shares K/V heads across queries, sliding-window attention that discards distant entries, and paged allocation that avoids fragmentation. The goal is more throughput and longer contexts on the same hardware.
102029: Distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher's outputs, typically matching the teacher's soft probability distribution, sometimes on generated data. The student retains much of the teacher's quality with a fraction of the latency and cost, which is how frontier capabilities get productized into cheap serving tiers.
102030: Mixture of Experts replaces the single dense feed-forward block with many expert blocks plus a router that sends each token to a few chosen experts, expanding parameter count while keeping per-token compute roughly constant. Models like Mixtral activate 2 of 8 experts per token, getting more capacity without proportional inference cost.
102031: Dense models route every token through all parameters; sparse MoE models activate a small subset per token via a router. Dense training is simpler and more stable; MoE offers better quality per unit of inference compute at the cost of needing to keep all experts in memory and managing routing balance.
102032: Flash Attention is an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that tiles the computation to fit in fast GPU memory, recomputes instead of storing large intermediates, and avoids materializing the full attention matrix. It yields large speedups and memory savings with identical outputs, enabling longer contexts and faster training.
102033: Cross-entropy loss compares the predicted probability distribution with the true next token, defined as the negative log probability assigned to the correct token. Minimizing it is maximum likelihood training; in LLMs it is computed over every position of the sequence in parallel during pretraining.
102034: GQA shares key and value heads across groups of query heads: instead of every query head having its own K/V, a small number of shared K/V heads serve all queries. It shrinks the KV cache several-fold, directly boosting throughput and batch size, while quality stays close to full multi-head attention. Llama 2 70B and Mistral use it.
102035: RoPE rotates each layer's query and key vectors by angles proportional to token position, so the dot product between a query and key depends only on their relative distance. It injects position without extra parameters, transfers better to longer sequences than learned absolute embeddings, and extends to long contexts via interpolation tricks.
102036: Layer normalization rescales each token's activations to zero mean and unit variance across its feature dimension, then applies learned gain and bias. It stabilizes training by keeping activation scale consistent regardless of depth or input, enabling higher learning rates and faster convergence in deep networks.
102037: RMSNorm is layer normalization without mean subtraction: it divides by the root-mean-square of the activations and applies a learned scale. It is cheaper and equally effective, which is why Llama-style models use it. BatchNorm normalizes across the batch, LayerNorm/RMSNorm across features, the latter being batch-independent and suited to sequence models.
103001: Prompt engineering is designing the model's input, instructions, examples, structure, and constraints, to reliably produce the behavior you want. It matters because LLMs are extremely sensitive to phrasing: clear roles, explicit output formats, and few-shot examples can dramatically change accuracy without any retraining. It is the cheapest and fastest optimization lever in LLM systems.
103002: Zero-shot prompting gives the task description only; few-shot adds a handful of input-output examples inside the prompt so the model imitates the pattern. Few-shot improves format compliance and accuracy on specialized tasks without training. Chain-of-thought asks the model to reason step by step before answering, substantially improving math, logic, and multi-step problems by letting computation unfold across generated tokens.
103003: To force structured output: show the exact schema in the prompt with a filled example, use lower temperature, prefer API features like JSON mode or function calling that constrain decoding, validate the result programmatically and retry with the error message appended, and keep instructions at the start with the schema repeated near the end for long prompts.
103004: Handle long documents with retrieval: chunk the document with overlap, embed chunks, retrieve only the relevant pieces into the context, and answer from those. Alternatives are hierarchical summarization, map-reduce over chunks, or long-context models with careful prompt placement. Never assume the model attended well to the middle of a very long prompt.
103005: Mitigate hallucination with grounding: give the model the source documents via RAG and instruct it to answer only from them, ask it to cite which chunk supports each claim, allow 'I don't know' explicitly, lower temperature, and validate outputs with checks or a second verifying pass. For admission of ignorance, few-shot examples of refusing when evidence is missing work well.
103006: Control verbosity with explicit length constraints in the prompt, such as 'answer in at most three sentences', by asking for bullet lists, and with few-shot examples at the desired length. Post-process by truncating sections, or use a cheaper model to compress. System prompts should fix a persona that includes response style.
103007: Prevent memorization leaks by fine-tuning only on data you are licensed to use, applying techniques like deduplication before training and appending canary strings to detect leakage, refusing prompts that solicit verbatim training text, and adding output filters that flag long exact matches against proprietary corpora. Alignment tuning and safety filtering further reduce regurgitation.
103008: Outdated code generation is a knowledge cutoff problem: fix it by grounding on current docs through retrieval (RAG over the libraries' latest documentation), providing tool access to type checkers and compilers that catch deprecated APIs, few-shot examples using current versions, or fine-tuning on modern code. Feed the compiler or linter errors back into the model for iterative repair.
103009: Fix tokenization of domain terms by adding them to the tokenizer vocabulary and continuing pretraining so the new embeddings learn, or by rephrasing with consistent spellings that tokenize well. In practice, adopting a tokenizer trained on domain text, such as code or biomedical corpora, or fine-tuning on domain data so the model is robust to fragmentation, are the standard paths.
103010: Manage KV cache memory with quantized caches, grouped-query or multi-query attention that shares K/V heads, sliding-window or sparse attention that bounds the effective cache, and paged attention that allocates cache memory in blocks to eliminate fragmentation. Also cap context length and evict stale conversations in serving.
103011: Scale beyond quadratic attention with sparse or local-window attention, linear attention variants, FlashAttention for constant-memory exact attention, chunked processing, hierarchical summarization with retrieval, and state-space or hybrid architectures. For RAG-style workloads, retrieving a few relevant chunks beats attending to everything.
104001: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) grounds an LLM in external knowledge: documents are chunked and embedded into a vector index, the user's query is embedded and similar chunks are retrieved, and the LLM answers using only those chunks, often citing them. It gives current, private, verifiable answers without retraining and reduces hallucination, at the cost of retrieval quality bottlenecks and more moving parts.
104002: RAG retrieves relevant knowledge at query time and is better for fresh, factual, verifiable content with citations; fine-tuning changes model weights and is better for style, format, and domain behavior, not for injecting facts that change. They complement each other: fine-tune for tone and structure, use RAG for knowledge. Start with RAG because it is easier to update and audit.
104003: A complete RAG pipeline: ingest documents, clean and chunk them with overlap, embed chunks with a retrieval model, store vectors plus metadata in a vector database, then at query time embed the query, retrieve top-k chunks (optionally rerank them), construct a prompt with the chunks and citations, generate the answer, and evaluate retrieval hit rate plus answer faithfulness.
104004: Chunking should preserve semantic units: split on headings, paragraphs, or sentences with 200-500 token chunks and 10-20% overlap, attach metadata like source and section, and for tables or code use structure-aware splitting. Chunks that are too small lose context, too big dilute relevance; evaluate retrieval quality against labeled questions when possible.
104005: Embeddings for retrieval come from bi-encoder models trained with contrastive loss so similar texts land close in vector space. Store them in a vector index like HNSW, retrieve with cosine or dot product, and remember the embedding model must match the query domain. Cross-encoder rerankers then rescore the top candidates jointly with the query for much better precision.
104006: A vector database stores embeddings with an approximate nearest neighbor index such as HNSW or IVF-PQ plus document metadata, supporting filtered vector search at scale. Examples include pgvector, FAISS, Milvus, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Pinecone. Choice hinges on scale, filtering needs, ops burden, and whether you want it colocated with relational data.
104007: Hybrid search combines keyword (BM25) and vector similarity, fusing results with reciprocal rank fusion or weighted scores. BM25 catches exact identifiers, codes, and rare terms that embeddings blur; vectors catch paraphrases and meaning. Together they substantially raise retrieval quality, which is why most production RAG systems are hybrid.
104008: Reranking takes the top-k retrieved candidates and rescores them with a stronger, slower model, usually a cross-encoder that jointly encodes query and chunk, then keeps the best few for generation. It fixes the precision loss of fast first-stage retrieval at modest cost, often the single highest-ROI upgrade to a RAG pipeline.
104009: Evaluate RAG in two layers: retrieval metrics like hit rate, MRR, and nDCG against labeled relevant chunks; and generation metrics like faithfulness (answers supported by retrieved context), answer relevance, and citation accuracy. Use LLM-as-judge with human spot checks, build a golden question set, and monitor drift in production with user feedback.
104010: Grounding means constraining the model to answer strictly from provided source chunks, quoting or citing them. Implement it with explicit instructions, structured prompts with numbered chunks, citation requirements per sentence, and post-hoc verification that each claim is entailed by a cited chunk. Faithfulness evaluation quantifies how well it works.
104011: Chunk size controls the granularity-relevance tradeoff: small chunks are precise but lose context, large chunks preserve context but dilute embeddings and waste tokens. Overlap mitigates boundary splits. Tune size by measuring retrieval hit rate and answer faithfulness on a question set; 300-500 tokens with 10-15% overlap is a common starting point.
104012: Metadata filtering narrows retrieval by attributes like source, date, tenant, or document type before or during vector search. It is essential for multi-tenant systems and freshness-aware answers, and it prevents one department's documents from leaking into another's answers. Store metadata alongside vectors and enforce filters server-side.
104013: Production RAG challenges: retrieval quality on ambiguous queries, index freshness versus re-embedding costs, multi-tenant permission enforcement, prompt injection through malicious documents, latency budgets with rerankers, evaluation of hallucinations, and cost management of embeddings plus generation. Solve with hybrid search, incremental indexing, ACL-aware retrieval, sanitization, caching, and continuous golden-set evaluation.
104014: Query rewriting transforms user queries into retrieval-friendly ones: expanding acronyms, decomposing multi-part questions, generating HyDE-style hypothetical answers to embed, or rewriting conversational context into standalone queries. It dramatically improves recall when users type short or ambiguous queries, at the cost of an extra LLM call that can be cached.
104015: Reduce hallucination in RAG by retrieving better (hybrid search plus reranking), instructing the model to answer only from context and cite it, lowering temperature, allowing 'not found in documents' answers, verifying claim-level entailment before display, and collecting user feedback loops. Never rely on prompting alone when facts matter.
105001: An AI agent is an LLM-driven system that perceives, plans, and acts: it takes a goal, decides which tools to call with what arguments, observes results, and iterates until the goal is met. The core loop is reason, act, observe, repeat, with memory and guardrails around it. Agents differ from single completions by maintaining state and taking multi-step actions in the world.
105002: Tool calling works by describing available functions with JSON schemas to the model; the model returns a structured call with a name and arguments; the host executes it and returns the result as a message; the model continues reasoning with the observation. Modern APIs constrain decoding to valid schemas, making the loop reliable enough for production.
105003: The ReAct pattern interleaves Reasoning and Acting: the model writes a thought about what to do next, chooses a tool call, receives the observation, and reflects again. This explicit chain makes the agent's decision process auditable and improves multi-step task success versus raw action selection, because each step is grounded in visible reasoning.
105004: Planning can be one-shot, where the model writes a full plan up front then executes, or dynamic, where it replans after each observation. Dynamic planning handles surprises better; one-shot is cheaper and more predictable. Complexity arises from error recovery, dead ends, and cost control, so production agents cap steps, add checkpoints, and prefer deterministic workflows over free-form loops when reliability matters.
105005: Agent memory splits into short-term context, the working conversation and scratchpad, and long-term stores, typically vector databases for semantic memory, key-value stores for facts and preferences, and episodic logs for retrieval. Memory is written after or during tasks, retrieved by similarity or recency, and summarized to fit context windows.
105006: Multi-agent systems split a complex goal among specialized roles, such as planner, coder, critic, and researcher, communicating through messages or shared state. Benefits are modularity, parallelism, and specialization; risks are compounding errors, runaway costs, and debugging difficulty. Simpler orchestration with deterministic workflows often beats full autonomy in production.
105007: Agent reliability comes from engineering: typed tool schemas with validation, retries with error feedback, step budgets and timeouts, sandboxed execution for code and shell tools, deterministic workflows for known paths, eval suites replaying recorded tasks, human approval gates for destructive actions, and full tracing of every step. Treat agents as distributed systems, not chatbots.
105008: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting models to tools and data sources: servers expose tools, resources, and prompts over a common protocol, and clients like IDEs or agent runtimes discover and call them uniformly. It decouples tool providers from applications, so the same MCP server works across different agent platforms, avoiding bespoke integrations.
105009: Guardrails for agents: least-privilege credentials per tool, read-only by default with explicit write approvals, sandboxing code execution and network access, input sanitization against prompt injection from tool outputs and web pages, output validation before actions, spend and step limits, and audit logs of every call. Human-in-the-loop for anything irreversible.
105010: Prompt injection is malicious text in data, emails, web pages, documents, that hijacks the LLM's instructions, making it leak data or call tools harmfully. Defenses: separate system instructions from untrusted content structurally, treat tool outputs as untrusted, sanitize or sandbox content, restrict tool permissions so a hijacked model stays low-risk, use injection detection classifiers, and keep humans in the loop for sensitive actions. No single defense is complete; layer them.
106001: Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on task-specific data so it adapts behavior, style, or format. Use it when prompting and RAG cannot achieve the needed consistency, latency, or cost, such as strict output schemas or domain-specific tone. Do not use it to inject frequently changing facts; retrieval serves that better.
106002: Full fine-tuning updates all weights, giving the best quality ceiling but requiring GPU memory for optimizer states, roughly 4-8x model size, and risking catastrophic forgetting. PEFT methods like LoRA freeze the base and train small adapters, cutting trainable parameters by orders of magnitude with near-equal quality for most adaptation tasks. Choose full for major behavior shifts, LoRA for efficient specialization.
106003: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the pretrained weights and learns two low-rank matrices A and B per target layer, adding BA as a delta: the update has rank r much smaller than the dimensions. Only A and B train, shrinking memory and checkpoint size enormously; multiple LoRAs can share one base model and be hot-swapped per customer.
106004: QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit (NF4) and trains LoRA adapters on top, making fine-tuning of large models feasible on single GPUs. The 4-bit storage with 16-bit compute via careful dequantization keeps quality close to full fine-tuning. It democratized customization of 30-70B models.
106005: Instruction tuning fine-tunes on instruction-response pairs so the base model learns to follow requests rather than just continue text. RLHF then aligns outputs with human preferences: train a reward model on human comparisons, then optimize the policy against it with PPO or use DPO, which optimizes directly on preference pairs without a separate reward model. This is the recipe behind chat models.
106006: Catastrophic forgetting is when fine-tuning on narrow data erodes general capabilities. Mitigate it by mixing general data into the fine-tune, using low learning rates and few epochs, preferring LoRA with small rank over full fine-tuning, and evaluating on both the target task and a general benchmark before shipping.
106007: Prepare fine-tuning data as diverse, representative, high-quality examples in the exact production format: consistent instruction and output schema, deduplicated, human-reviewed, covering edge cases and refusals. A few hundred to a few thousand excellent examples usually beat a million noisy ones; split a holdout for evaluation and measure against the base model.
106008: Quantization represents weights with fewer bits, 8-bit or 4-bit, using schemes like NF4 or GPTQ that map values to learned levels, shrinking memory several-fold for inference and enabling QLoRA training. Quality loss at 4-bit with modern methods is small for most uses. Lower precision mainly risks degradation on outlier-sensitive layers, which mixed precision schemes protect.
107001: Vector databases index high-dimensional embeddings for fast approximate nearest neighbor search with metadata filtering. HNSW builds a navigable small-world graph giving high recall and low latency with more memory; IVF-PQ clusters vectors and compresses them with product quantization for billion-scale storage at lower recall. Pick based on recall requirements, scale, update frequency, and filtering needs.
107002: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is a multi-layer graph where upper layers are sparse for long jumps and lower layers are dense for fine search; queries greedily descend from the top. It achieves excellent recall-latency tradeoffs and is the default index in most vector databases, at the cost of memory for the graph and slower builds.
107003: Product quantization compresses vectors by splitting them into subvectors, each quantized to its nearest centroid in a small codebook, storing just codes instead of floats. This cuts memory 10-100x with a modest recall loss and enables billion-vector indexes on one machine, often combined with IVF clustering and rescoring for accuracy.
107004: Choose the embedding model by matching domain and language, checking retrieval benchmark scores like MTEB, balancing dimension versus storage and speed, verifying supported context length, and testing on your own labeled queries before committing. The embedding model defines your retrieval ceiling; swapping later means re-embedding everything, so benchmark early.
107005: Cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors, normalizing away magnitude; dot product also weights magnitude, and Euclidean distance measures straight-line separation. For normalized embeddings all three rank identically. Use cosine for text similarity; dot product when vector norms carry meaning, like popularity signals.
107006: Embeddings drift when you change the embedding model or version: old and new vectors live in different spaces and cannot be mixed. Handle it by versioning the index, re-embedding in background with dual-read during migration, and pinning the model version in config. Also monitor query-vector distribution drift in production as content shifts.
108001: AI system design questions test whether you can assemble LLMs, retrieval, tools, and evaluation into a product that is accurate, fast, safe, and affordable. A strong answer structures the problem: requirements and constraints, data pipeline, retrieval and generation architecture, evaluation strategy, latency and cost budget, safety and permissions, and an iterative improvement plan, then reasons about trade-offs out loud.
108002: A production RAG chatbot architecture: ingestion pipeline that chunks, embeds, and indexes documents with ACL metadata; hybrid retrieval with reranking; a generation service with strict grounding prompts and citations; evaluation harness with golden questions; observability with tracing per stage; caching of embeddings and frequent answers; and feedback collection. Scale each component independently and version everything.
108003: Design a document Q&A system with permission-aware ingestion so ACLs ride along as metadata, filtered retrieval enforcing user permissions server-side, hybrid search plus rerankers for quality, citation-required generation, and an evaluation set spanning departments. Cache aggressively by content hash and monitor unanswerable-rate as a key metric.
108004: Design a code assistant with retrieval over the repository index, AST-aware chunking, tool access to compilers and tests for validation, low-latency small models for completions with larger models for chat, and feedback capture on accepted suggestions. Latency is the primary constraint, so cache prefixes, stream tokens, and keep the retrieval loop local.
108005: LLM latency breaks into time-to-first-token, dominated by prefill over the prompt, and per-token decode speed, dominated by memory bandwidth. Reduce TTFT by shrinking prompts with retrieval instead of dumping context, caching, and faster hardware; reduce decode time with speculative decoding, quantization, KV cache optimization, and batching. Stream tokens so users perceive progress.
108006: Cut LLM costs with prompt compression and retrieval instead of huge prompts, model routing that sends easy requests to small cheap models, response and prefix caching, batching, quantized serving, and self-hosting open-weight models at steady high volume. Measure cost per resolved request, not per token, to target optimizations.
108007: Scale LLM inference with continuous batching that packs requests dynamically, paged KV cache allocation, tensor parallelism across GPUs, quantization for memory bandwidth, speculative decoding with draft models, and prefix caching for shared system prompts. Throughput per GPU and cost per million tokens are the north-star metrics.
109001: LLMOps applies DevOps discipline to LLM products: versioning prompts, models, and indexes; evaluation gates in CI; deployment with canary and rollback; observability tracing every prompt, retrieval, and generation; cost and latency monitoring; and feedback loops that turn production failures into test cases. It differs from MLOps by centering on prompts, retrieval quality, and non-deterministic outputs.
109002: Monitor an LLM application across quality (hallucination rate, citation accuracy, task success, user feedback), performance (TTFT, tokens per second, timeout rate), cost (tokens and dollars per request, per user, per feature), and safety (refusal rate, injection attempts, policy violations). Log traces per stage, sample for human review, and alert on drift.
109003: Version prompts like code: store them in the repo, parameterize variables, review changes with eval runs against golden sets, and deploy them with the same canary discipline as models. Track every production call against the prompt version that produced it, so regressions are attributable and rollback is a config change.
109004: A/B test LLM features by routing a fraction of traffic to the variant, predefining metrics like task success and user satisfaction, running long enough for significance, and watching guardrails like latency and cost. Because outputs are non-deterministic, evaluate with both automated graders and sampled human judgment; keep a holdout to catch regressions.
109005: Handle model updates by pinning versions, re-running the evaluation suite against every candidate model, canarying before full rollout, and keeping prompt variants per model since behavior shifts. Maintain a fallback chain to the previous model on failure, and treat capability changes as product changes with review.
109006: LLM caching layers: exact response cache keyed by full prompt hash, semantic cache that returns previous answers for similar queries with a similarity threshold, prefix cache for shared system prompts at the provider level, and chunk or embedding caches in RAG. Semantic caching needs careful thresholds to avoid wrong hits; always log cache provenance for debugging.
109007: Trace LLM systems by logging every stage: incoming request, prompt version, retrieved chunks with scores, raw completion, tool calls, latency per stage, and token counts. Store traces correlated by request id so any user complaint can be replayed exactly. This is the backbone for debugging, evaluation, and cost attribution.
110001: Evaluate LLM outputs with a layered strategy: deterministic checks for format and safety, reference-based metrics like exact match or BLEU/ROUGE when ground truth exists, LLM-as-judge with rubrics for open-ended quality, and human evaluation sampled from production. Combine automated metrics with periodic human audits because each alone is gameable.
110002: LLM-as-judge uses a strong model with a detailed rubric to score outputs, often pairwise to reduce position bias. It scales evaluation cheaply but has biases: length, self-preference, and position. Mitigate by swapping option order, using rubric anchors with examples, calibrating against human labels, and reserving human review for disagreements.
110003: Benchmark overfitting happens when you tune against a public test set until scores look great while real performance lags. Prevent it with private holdout sets, fresh task variants, rotating evaluation data, and measuring production outcomes rather than benchmark numbers. Treat public benchmarks as smoke tests, not proof.
110004: Test a RAG system with a golden question set mapped to relevant chunks: measure retrieval hit rate and MRR for the retriever, faithfulness and answer relevance for the generator, plus citation precision. Expand the set continuously from production failures, and run it in CI so retrieval or prompt changes cannot silently regress quality.
110005: Regression testing for prompts and models: maintain a versioned eval suite of tasks, edge cases, refusals, and format checks; run it on every prompt, model, or retrieval change; gate deployments on score thresholds; and diff failures against the previous version. Store traces so production incidents convert into new test cases.
111001: Guard against jailbreaks with layered defenses: policy-tuned models, input classifiers for known attack patterns, structural separation of instructions from user data, output filtering, and permission-constrained tools so even a successful jailbreak has limited blast radius. Monitor production for novel patterns and update filters continuously; assume some will get through.
111002: Prevent PII leakage by classifying and redacting sensitive data before it reaches the model or logs, restricting what the model can return via output filters and allowlists, enforcing data residency and access controls per tenant, and auditing traces for accidental retention. Privacy engineering applies to prompts, completions, embeddings, and logs alike.
111003: Fairness in LLMs means equitable quality across demographic groups and languages: evaluate performance disaggregated by group, balance training and evaluation data, and test for biased associations in outputs. Mitigations include inclusive data curation, bias benchmarks, alignment policies, and human review for high-stakes decisions. Publish limitations honestly.
111004: Transparency for LLM products means telling users they are talking to AI, disclosing known limitations, citing sources for factual claims, and documenting model, data, and evaluation choices. Explainability adds mechanisms like citations, retrieval evidence, and reasoning traces that show why an output was produced, which also aids debugging and audits.
111005: Build responsible AI practices into the lifecycle: model and data documentation, risk assessments per feature, red-teaming and bias evaluation before launch, usage policies and enforcement, human oversight for consequential decisions, incident response with rollback, and continuous monitoring. Make it an engineering discipline with owners and gates, not a policy document.
112001: Multimodal models process multiple modalities, text plus images, audio, or video, typically by encoding non-text inputs into the same embedding space the language model attends over. Vision-language models feed image patches as tokens; speech models use audio encoders like Whisper's. Applications include image understanding, document AI, video search, and voice agents.
112002: Vision-language models combine a vision encoder, like ViT producing patch embeddings, with an LLM through a projection layer or cross-attention, trained on image-text pairs for captioning, VQA, and instruction following. The LLM reasons over visual tokens as it would over text, enabling charts, screenshots, and document understanding.
112003: Document AI pipelines parse layout, OCR or use native vision models, chunk by structure, and either extract fields with schema-constrained outputs or enable RAG over documents with tables preserved as structured text. Key challenges are tables, handwriting, and multi-page context; evaluation uses field-level accuracy rather than free-text similarity.
113001: Scale AI infrastructure with tensor and pipeline parallelism to shard models across GPUs, quantization and KV-cache optimization to raise per-GPU throughput, continuous batching for utilization, autoscaling with queue-depth triggers, and tiered serving that routes traffic across model sizes. Multi-region deployment plus caching fronts the fleet for global latency.
113002: GPU utilization for LLMs is memory-bandwidth-bound during decode, so raise arithmetic intensity with bigger batches, quantized weights and KV caches, and FlashAttention-class kernels; keep GPUs fed with continuous batching and prefetch. Track MFU, tokens per second per GPU, and cost per million tokens as the core efficiency metrics.
113003: Self-host open-weight models when data cannot leave your perimeter, volume makes per-token pricing dominate, latency control matters, or you need custom weights. You accept ops burden: model serving, scaling, security patching, and evaluation. Most companies start with APIs and move the predictable high-volume traffic to self-hosted open models.
114001: Practical LLM coding tasks reward structure: define the interface and schemas first, write the prompt as code with versions and tests, stream outputs with timeout and retry handling, validate responses programmatically, and log traces for debugging. Use the provider's structured-output or function-calling features rather than parsing free text, and unit-test edge cases like empty inputs and token limits.
114002: Implement RAG retrieval in code by embedding the query with the same model used for documents, querying the vector store with top-k plus metadata filters, optionally reranking with a cross-encoder, and assembling the prompt with numbered chunks for citation. Handle empty retrieval with a graceful refusal path and cache embeddings by content hash.
114003: Build a streaming chat backend with SSE or WebSockets, storing conversation state server-side, forwarding provider token streams to the client, applying moderation on input and output, persisting traces for evaluation, and handling cancellation when users stop generation. Idempotency keys prevent double-billing on retries.
114004: A tool-calling loop: declare functions with JSON schemas, call the model, parse the returned tool calls, execute them in a sandbox with timeouts, append results as messages, and loop until the model stops or a step budget hits. Validate arguments against schemas, catch execution errors and feed them back as observations, and log every step for replay.
115001: Scenario: your RAG chatbot answers wrong confidently. Diagnose in layers: was the right chunk retrieved (retrieval hit rate), was it in the prompt and attended (context position, chunking), did the model ignore it (prompt clarity, conflicting instructions), or is it a formatting/citation bug. Fix retrieval first, then prompts, then add faithfulness checks; log traces to attribute failures precisely.
115002: Scenario: hallucination report. Reproduce with the trace, check whether evidence existed in retrieval, add or fix the missing source, tighten grounding prompts and citations, add entailment verification for the affected surface, and add the case to the golden eval set. Communicate the fix as a measured change: hallucination rate before and after on the eval suite.
115003: Scenario: latency complaints. Measure the stage breakdown: retrieval time, prefill TTFT, decode speed. Then apply targeted fixes: cache embeddings and frequent answers, shrink prompts via retrieval, stream tokens to the UI, quantize or batch the serving layer, and move rerankers behind a strict latency budget. Set an SLO, alert on it, and report percentiles, not averages.
115004: Behavioral answers for AI roles should follow STAR: the Situation and Task ground the story, the Action emphasizes your specific engineering decisions, model choices, evaluation designs, and trade-offs, and the Result quantifies impact with metrics like latency, cost, quality lift, or adoption. Prepare three to five deep project stories and map them to leadership, conflict, failure, and ownership questions.
116001: Give a 90-second structured pitch: present role and one relevant achievement, then two or three past wins with numbers that map to this job, and close with why this role is the right next step. Keep it confident and specific, never recite your resume line by line. Example: 'I am a data scientist with two years in churn modeling, where I cut churn 12 percent; before that I built the analytics dashboard my college placement cell still uses. I am now looking to apply that in a larger ML product team, which is why this role excites me.'
116002: Pick a narrative thread, not the whole document: education, then each role with one accomplishment and one skill gained, showing a logical progression toward this job. Spend the most time on what is most relevant to the interviewer's team and end at why this position is the natural next move.
116003: Match three specifics of the job description to three proof points you own: a skill with a project, a domain with experience, and a trait with evidence, then add a commitment line about ramping fast. Close with enthusiasm for the team's mission rather than generic 'I am hardworking' claims.
116004: Choose two technical and one soft strength that the role actually needs, each with a one-line proof: 'I turn messy requirements into working first drafts fast; my last model shipped in three weeks from kickoff.' Avoid cliches without evidence and avoid strengths irrelevant to the job.
116005: Name a real, non-critical weakness and show the correcting system: 'I used to go deep polishing alone too early; now I share rough work within 48 hours and timebox refinement, which improved my feedback cycles.' Never use humble-brags like 'I work too hard' — interviewers hear those all day.
116006: Show ambition anchored to the path this role sits on: growing from strong individual contributor to owning projects end to end, deepening expertise in the team's domain, maybe mentoring. Keep the focus on growth at this company rather than naming titles, timelines, or aspirations that point away from the job.
116007: Prove you researched them: cite one product, technical blog post, value, or recent development that genuinely interests you, and connect it to your experience and goals. Structure as 'what I admire, what I bring, what I want to learn here.' Generic answers signal mass applications.
116008: Stay positive and future-focused: seeking larger scale, new domains, or growth that your current role cannot offer. Never badmouth your employer, manager, or colleagues — the interviewer assumes you will describe them the same way someday. End on what attracts you to this opportunity.
116009: Use STAR: a real challenge with stakes, the specific actions you personally took, and a quantified result. Pick a work or project example, not a personal crisis. 'Our model degraded after deployment; I built a monitoring pipeline, found feature drift, retrained with rolling windows, and restored accuracy within a week.'
116010: Choose a real failure with lessons that changed your behavior: 'I shipped a model without checking for data leakage; validation collapsed in production. I now run leakage audits before every release and taught my team the checklist.' Own it fully, skip blame, and show the corrective system you built.
116011: Pick a professional disagreement, show you listened first and found common ground: 'My stakeholder wanted a complex model; I showed the accuracy-versus-latency trade-off with data, proposed a phased approach, and we shipped the simple version first.' Emphasize empathy, direct communication, and the shared goal rather than winning.
116012: Leadership without a title counts: leading a project, unblocking a stuck team, mentoring a junior, or driving a decision with data. Use STAR and highlight how you aligned people, not just what you delivered.
116013: Show collaboration mechanics: how you divided work, communicated progress, handled disagreement, and supported others. Quantify the outcome and credit teammates genuinely — 'we' for success, 'I' for the specific actions you owned.
116014: Describe a real system, not a platitude: prioritizing by impact, splitting work into milestones, communicating early when scope is at risk, and staying calm. Give one example where this system delivered under a real deadline.
116015: Show you treat feedback as data: listen fully, ask clarifying questions, thank them, and act on it with a concrete example of a change you made. Never get defensive; interviewers are testing coachability, which predicts growth.
116016: Be honest and specific to the role: solving hard problems with data, seeing users benefit from your model, continuous learning. Connect motivation to what the job actually offers daily, so the answer reads as genuine fit rather than rehearsed idealism.
116017: Deflect gracefully first if you can: ask for their budgeted range. If pressed, give a researched range from market data for the role and city, anchored slightly above your target, and stay flexible on total compensation. 'Based on market data for this role in this city, I am looking at X to Y, and I am open to discussing the full package.'
116018: Honesty works here: a calm yes shows you are a credible candidate, and saying the role's fit attracts you most signals genuine interest. Never brag about offers as leverage; never lie, since it surfaces eventually.
116019: Always ask two or three: 'What does success look like in the first six months?', 'How does the team handle model deployment and monitoring?', 'What do you enjoy most about working here?' No questions signals low interest; salary-only questions at this stage signal wrong priorities.
116020: Answer directly and honestly about your constraints first, then show flexibility where it exists. If relocation is hard, say so clearly and ask about hybrid options rather than over-promising and quitting later.
116021: Keep it brief, factual, and forward-moving: what you did in the gap, such as upskilling with courses, projects, freelancing, or family responsibilities, and how it makes you sharper now. No apologies, no oversharing; steer back to your readiness for this role.
116022: Prepare three facts: what the company does and for whom, one recent product, funding, or news item, and how the team you are joining fits the mission. Deliver them naturally inside your 'why here' answer rather than reciting like a quiz.
116023: Pick one with measurable impact and a clear personal contribution: 'I built the demand forecasting model that cut stockouts 18 percent across 40 stores.' Use STAR, quantify everything, and explain why it mattered to the business, not just to you.
116024: Choose three traits the role rewards, each with a one-line anecdote: reliable under deadlines, curious about tooling, calm in incidents. Quoting a past review or a mentor's phrase adds authenticity.
116025: Pick something real that transfers to this job, such as ownership, mentoring, or the modeling problems, and explain why. It signals what environment you seek; pair it with what you hope to find here.
116026: Choose a neutral structural constraint, like limited data infrastructure or slow release cycles, not people, and show what you did about it and what you learned. Never badmouth; keep it to one dislike and pivot to what you are seeking.
116027: Turn it into a growth story: coursework built foundations, and projects or self-learning added the practical stack. Show the bridge artifacts, like certifications, Kaggle projects, or open-source work, that prove continuous learning.
116028: Describe a real method: impact versus effort ranking, stakeholder alignment on deadlines, breaking work into shippable slices, and communicating trade-offs early. Give one concrete example where prioritization saved a deliverable.
116029: Align honestly with what the company offers: collaborative, data-driven, autonomous with clear ownership. Avoid listing perks or contradicting the reality of the team, since interviewers check fit signals here.
116030: Mention one or two genuine interests briefly and connect skills where natural: chess and strategy, blogging and communication, sports and teamwork. Authenticity beats impressiveness; a short warm answer keeps it human.
116031: Show commitment and maturity: you evaluate opportunities on growth, learning, and team, not only money, and job-hopping purely for small raises damages long-term growth. Express that you would raise concerns openly internally first. This tests loyalty signals, so avoid both rigid vows and cavalier talk.
116032: Tests structured persuasion: ask about their needs first, match features to those needs, handle one objection, and close with a ask. 'How often do you sign important documents? A pen you trust matters then; this one writes smoothly and never leaks. Shall we say you will try it this week?' Structure matters far more than the close.
